parts.title: Part 1
parts.context: A woman phones about dog training classes.
script: Hello, Good Dog Training, Jake speaking.
Hi. I'd like to book some training classes for my dog.
Sure. Can I have your name?
Alice Turner. T, U, R, N, E, R.
And what breed is your dog?
Is there any particular problem you'd like help with?
She's very friendly, but she pulls on the lead all the time. Walks are exhausting.
That's very common at that age. I'd recommend our puppy class rather than the basic class, which is for older dogs.
Thursday evenings, from seven until eight, in the village hall on Station Road.
Plenty of small treats, and her favourite toy, so she stays interested.
It's seventy-two pounds for six sessions.
Do you need anything from me before we start?
Yes, please bring her vaccination certificate to the first class. We can't accept dogs without one.

parts.title: Part 2
parts.context: A council spokesperson describes a new tram line.
script: Good evening. I'm Rachel Green from the city council, and I'm here to tell you about the new Line Two tram service.
We had hoped to open on the first of September, but final safety checks took longer than expected, so the line will now open on the fifteenth of September.
Trams will run every six minutes at peak times and every ten minutes during the rest of the day.
Please note that you can't buy tickets from the driver. You can buy them using our app or from machines at every stop.
Bicycles are not allowed on trams, except for folding bikes, which can be carried at any time.
Now, the stops. Riverside is the closest stop for the university.
Park Gate is right next to the zoo, which we expect to be very popular with families.
Millfield is the stop for the football stadium, and extra trams will run on match days.
The Harbour stop is just a short walk from the beach.
Northgate serves the main hospital. There's a covered walkway from the platform to the entrance.
And Kingsway is the stop for the new shopping centre.

parts.title: Part 3
parts.context: Two students, Jade and Omar, discuss their study of recycling in student halls.
script: Jade, let's write up our recycling project. Why did we choose the student halls again?
Because the university's figures showed the halls have the lowest recycling rate on the whole campus.
Right. And we observed the contents of the bins every week for four weeks.
Yes. In our survey, the main reason students gave for not recycling properly was that the signs on the bins were confusing.
So our intervention was to replace them with colour-coded bins with pictures of what goes in each one.
And the main result was that contamination, putting the wrong things in the recycling bins, fell a lot.
Let's check the numbers. Before the intervention, twenty-two percent of waste was recycled.
And afterwards it was forty-one percent. Almost double.
The most common wrong item in the recycling bins was coffee cups, because people think they're paper, but they have a plastic lining.
We surveyed a hundred and fifty students in total.
And the next step is to present our findings to the accommodation office, so they can introduce the new bins in all the halls.

parts.title: Part 4
parts.context: A lecture on the Aral Sea.
script: Today's lecture is about one of the worst environmental disasters of the twentieth century: the shrinking of the Aral Sea in Central Asia.
In 1960, the Aral Sea, which lies between Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan, was the fourth largest lake in the world. It was fed by two great rivers, the Amu Darya and the Syr Darya.
In the 1960s, the Soviet government decided to divert water from these rivers to irrigate the desert, mainly to grow cotton. The plan succeeded in producing cotton, but it starved the lake of water.
The lake began to shrink rapidly. By the 2010s, it had lost around ninety percent of its water, and it had split into several smaller lakes.

The fishing industry collapsed. The port town of Muynak, spelled M, U, Y, N, A, K, once surrounded by water, is now more than a hundred kilometres from the shore, and rusting fishing boats lie in the sand.
The exposed lake bed has become a desert. Strong winds pick up dust containing salt and pesticides from the old cotton fields and carry it across the region.
This has had serious effects on health. Local people suffer from high rates of respiratory illness and certain types of cancer.

There has been some recovery in the north. In 2005, Kazakhstan completed the Kok-Aral dam, which keeps water from the Syr Darya in the northern part of the lake. Within a year, the water level rose by about three metres.
Fish have returned, including carp, and fishing has started again.
On the dry seabed in the south, scientists are planting a desert shrub called saxaul, spelled S, A, X, A, U, L, to stabilise the soil and reduce dust storms.

passages.title: The Rosetta Stone
paragraphs: In July 1799, French soldiers rebuilding a fort near the town of Rashid, known to Europeans as Rosetta, on the Nile Delta, uncovered a large slab of dark stone covered in writing. The soldiers were part of Napoleon Bonaparte's military campaign in Egypt, which was accompanied by scholars, and the officer in charge quickly recognised that the stone might be important.

The stone carries a decree issued by a council of priests in 196 BC, praising the young king Ptolemy V and listing the honours to be given to him. What made it so valuable was that the same text was written three times, in three different scripts. At the top were Egyptian hieroglyphs, the ancient picture writing used on temples and tombs. In the middle was Demotic, a script used for everyday documents. At the bottom was ancient Greek, which scholars could already read.

The stone did not stay in French hands for long. After British forces defeated the French in Egypt, the stone was handed over to Britain in 1801 under the terms of the Treaty of Alexandria. It was taken to London and has been displayed in the British Museum since 1802.

Because the Greek section could be read, scholars hoped the stone would unlock the meaning of hieroglyphs, which no one had been able to read for more than a thousand years. Progress was slow. The English scientist Thomas Young made important early advances. He showed that the oval shapes, called cartouches, enclosed the names of rulers, and he identified the sounds of several signs in the name of Ptolemy.

The decisive breakthrough came from the French scholar Jean-François Champollion, who announced his decipherment in 1822. Champollion had studied many ancient languages, including Coptic, a later form of the Egyptian language written in an alphabet based on Greek. His knowledge of Coptic allowed him to show that hieroglyphs represented both sounds and ideas, and that they recorded the language of ancient Egypt.

Today, the Rosetta Stone is one of the most visited objects in the British Museum. In recent years, Egyptian officials and archaeologists have called for it to be returned to Egypt, as part of a wider debate about objects taken from other countries during the colonial era.

passages.title: How Animals Sleep
paragraphs: Sleep appears to be almost universal in the animal kingdom. Mammals, birds, reptiles, fish and insects all show periods of reduced activity and responsiveness that scientists recognise as sleep. In 2017, researchers even found that the upside-down jellyfish Cassiopea, an animal without a brain, enters a sleep-like state at night: it pulses more slowly, responds more slowly to stimulation and, if kept awake, becomes less active the following day.

Some animals have evolved remarkable ways of sleeping. Dolphins, which must surface regularly to breathe, sleep with only one half of the brain at a time, a pattern known as unihemispheric sleep. While one half rests, the other remains alert, and the dolphin keeps the eye connected to the waking half open, allowing it to watch for predators and stay in contact with its group.

Birds that spend long periods at sea face a similar challenge. In a 2016 study, scientists attached small devices to frigatebirds, which can fly for weeks without landing, to record their brain activity. They found that the birds did sleep in flight, sometimes with one half of the brain and sometimes with both, but only for around 42 minutes a day in total, compared with more than 12 hours a day when they were on land.

There is huge variation in how much animals sleep. A study of wild African elephants in Botswana, published in 2017, used activity monitors placed in the elephants' trunks and found that they slept for only about two hours a day, the least of any mammal recorded. Elephants sometimes went without sleep for nearly two days while moving long distances, possibly to avoid predators or poachers.

At the other extreme, the little brown bat can sleep for up to 20 hours a day. Large grazing animals such as giraffes and horses tend to sleep relatively little, perhaps because they need to spend many hours eating and must remain alert to danger.

Why sleep exists at all is still debated. Sleep appears to help animals form and store memories, and research in mice published in 2013 suggested that during sleep the brain clears away waste products through a network called the glymphatic system. That even a brainless jellyfish needs something like sleep suggests that its origins may be very ancient, and its purposes more basic than scientists once thought.

passages.title: Free Money for Everyone?
paragraphs: The idea of a universal basic income, or UBI, is simple: every adult receives a regular cash payment from the government, whether or not they work, and without conditions. Unlike traditional welfare benefits, which are usually means-tested and require recipients to prove that they are looking for work, a UBI would be paid to everyone.

The idea is not new. In 1797, the political writer Thomas Paine proposed that every citizen should receive a payment funded by a tax on land, arguing that the earth was originally the common property of all. In the twentieth century, the economist Milton Friedman suggested a related idea, a 'negative income tax', under which people earning below a certain level would receive money from the government instead of paying tax.

Several experiments have tested the idea. Between 2017 and 2018, Finland gave 2,000 unemployed people a monthly payment of 560 euros, with no conditions attached. The effect on employment was small, but participants reported less stress and greater confidence in the future. In Kenya, a long-running experiment by a charity has provided regular payments to entire villages. Contrary to fears that people would waste the money, many recipients invested it, for example in livestock or small businesses.

Supporters argue that UBI will become increasingly necessary as automation and artificial intelligence change the labour market. If machines take over many tasks, they say, a guaranteed income could protect people from poverty and give them the security to retrain or start businesses. It would also be simpler to administer than complex benefit systems and would remove the stigma attached to claiming welfare.

Critics raise serious objections. The most obvious is cost: paying a meaningful income to every adult would require very large increases in taxes. Some worry that people would choose to work less, reducing the economy's output, and that a sudden increase in the money available to spend could push up prices. Others argue that giving the same amount to rich and poor alike is an inefficient use of public money.

In my view, the evidence so far is encouraging but limited. Most experiments have been small, short or restricted to particular groups, such as the unemployed, and cannot show what would happen if an entire country adopted a full UBI. I believe that governments should carry out further large-scale trials before deciding whether a universal income could work in practice. In the meantime, making existing welfare systems simpler and less punishing may achieve many of the same goals at lower cost.

task1.text: The line graph below shows the number of international tourist arrivals, in millions, in four regions of the world between 2000 and 2019. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant. Write at least 150 words.
model: The line graph shows the number of international tourist arrivals in Europe, Asia-Pacific, the Americas and Africa between 2000 and 2019.

Overall, tourist numbers increased in all four regions over the period. Europe received by far the most visitors throughout, while Asia-Pacific experienced the fastest growth, and Africa remained the least visited region.
In 2000, Europe welcomed 390 million international tourists, around three times as many as the Americas, with 128 million, and Asia-Pacific, with 110 million. Africa received just 26 million.

Over the next two decades, arrivals in Europe almost doubled, reaching 745 million in 2019, with particularly rapid growth after 2010. Asia-Pacific grew even faster in relative terms, overtaking the Americas by 2005 and more than tripling to 360 million by 2019. The Americas saw slower growth, to 219 million, while Africa's numbers rose to 70 million, almost three times the 2000 figure but still well below the other regions.

task2.text: Some people think that governments should spend money on supporting the arts, such as music, theatre and painting. Others believe this money should be spent on more important public services. Discuss both views and give your own opinion. Write at least 250 words.
model: Public money is limited, and governments must constantly decide how to divide it between competing needs. While some people believe that funding the arts is a luxury, others see it as an essential part of a healthy society. In my view, governments should continue to support the arts, although at a modest level compared with core services.

Those who oppose arts funding argue that public services such as healthcare, education and housing are more urgent. When hospitals are overcrowded and schools lack teachers, spending money on opera houses or art galleries can seem difficult to justify. They also point out that much art is enjoyed mainly by wealthier and better-educated people, so public subsidies may benefit those who need help least. Successful artists, they suggest, can rely on ticket sales and private sponsors.

However, there are strong arguments for public support. The arts help to preserve a nation's culture and identity, from traditional music to local theatre, much of which could not survive on commercial income alone. They also bring economic benefits, attracting tourists and supporting jobs in creative industries. Furthermore, publicly funded projects, such as free concerts or art programmes in schools, can make culture accessible to people who could never afford it otherwise, and participation in the arts has been linked to improved wellbeing.

In my opinion, the solution is balance. Essential services should always receive the largest share of public spending, but a small proportion should be set aside for the arts, with priority given to projects that reach young people and disadvantaged communities.
In conclusion, although public services must come first, I believe that modest government support for the arts is a worthwhile investment in a society's culture, economy and wellbeing.

speaking.cue:
Describe a historical place you have visited.
You should say:
- where it is
- when you visited it
- what you saw there
and explain how you felt about the visit.
speaking.cueModel: I'd like to talk about Paharpur, an ancient Buddhist monastery in the north-west of Bangladesh, which I visited on a school trip when I was about fifteen. It's a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and it dates back more than twelve hundred years, to the eighth century. Honestly, before we arrived, I wasn't expecting much. I thought it would just be some old bricks in a field. But when I actually saw it, I was amazed by the scale. In the centre, there's a huge temple built in a cross shape, rising in terraces, and around it there's a square of more than one hundred and seventy small cells where monks used to live and study. The walls are decorated with terracotta plaques showing animals, people and scenes from everyday life, and our guide explained what many of them meant. What struck me most was the idea that, more than a thousand years ago, this place was one of the most important centres of learning in Asia, with students coming from far away. It made me feel proud of our history, but also a little sad, because many of the plaques have been damaged and the site doesn't get as much attention as it deserves.
